newsitem.title: USA: Copper rise sharply on expectations of stock fall.
newsitem.headline: Copper rise sharply on expectations of stock fall.

text.p: Copper prices rose sharply Thursday amid speculation that the London Metal Exchange will announce another sharp cut in stocks Friday.
A decline in the dollar also helped copper as well as precious metals. Heating oil prices extended their gains in New York on forecasts for colder weather in the Northeast.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures rose 1.71 points to 238.74.
Many in the copper market were awaiting news on how much, if any, copper had moved into LME warehouses in Singapore.
LME stocks have fallen 56 percent to 121,175 metric tons in the past two months as metal has been relocated from Europe to the Far East and the United States.
"We still have mixed opinions how much copper is going to the Far East," said Rich Hirsch of Deutsche Morgan Greenfell.
"It's pretty apparent this stuff is not being purchased to be buried in a cave out there. It's going to be consumed sooner rather than later," he added.
December copper on New York's Commodity Exchange closed up 2.90 cents at 95.55 cents a pound.
Traders said the overnight weakness in the dollar led to buying in both base and precious metal markets.

"It's all the fault of the Japanese, talking the dollar down and the yen back up, which created some nervousness in world financial markets and resulted in some fund short covering in commodities," said Phil Tiger, commodities strategist for Smith Barney in Washington.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said Thursday he thought the dollar's correction from last year's sharp slide against the yen was about to end. The comments sent the dollar sharply lower.
Precious metals were also higher on dollar-related buying. COMEX December gold ended up 90 cents at $379.60 an ounce while silver closed 12 cents higher at $4.833 an ounce.
Heating oil prices extended their gains in New York as colder temperatures were seen hitting the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world, at a time when supplies are tight.
Traders said, however, that the larger trend for oil prices was still bearish.

"The basic bear trend is still in place, but we have some good fundamentals surrounding heat right now, like colder temperatures and a drop in distillate supply," said John Bradberry, vice president at Continental Ozark Inc., a petroleum distributor in Arkansas.
Heating oil for December delivery settled up 0.44 cent at 66.89 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Jon Davis, meteorologist with Smith Barney, forecast temperatures would be 10 to 14 degrees below normal from Sunday to Tuesday in the northeastern United States.
Heating oil buoyed crude and gasoline, which traders said would have slipped if heating oil had not propped up other oil prices.
"There was plenty of downside in crude," said a trader.
December crude settled up 5 cents at $22.74 a barrel while December gasoline ended up 0.17 cent at 63.80 cents a gallon.
